pullQuote: I’d choose A2UI for its catalog-constrained agent interface and native renderers, while keeping visual design and authorization under application control.
testimonial: I would choose A2UI because its Catalogs and incremental surface updates give agents a bounded interface vocabulary without requiring generated executable UI code. Its Agent SDK, two-way data binding, and bidirectional function RPC let me connect human interactions and agent operations across web, Flutter, and SwiftUI. I would still enforce authorization in application services and test each renderer’s accessibility behavior rather than treating schema validation as a security guarantee. Compared with Tamagui, I accept more catalog implementation and renderer-version coordination in exchange for an explicit, framework-independent agent-to-interface contract.
evaluations:
**AI Elements** — Copy-in React components such as Tool and Confirmation make agent activity legible to people; Tool explicitly represents streaming, approval, completion, denial, and error states. That is a presentation layer, not a native renderer or shared application-operation contract. More importantly for a new project, the captured repository announces deprecation at the end of November 2026 and migration to shadcn/ui. I would use the successor for web conversation surfaces rather than make this repository my foundation; native components and application tools would remain separate work. Sources: [repository and migration notice](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements), [Tool documentation](https://elements.ai-sdk.dev/components/tool).

**Flutter** — A substantial alternative when one Dart codebase across mobile, desktop, and web is the overriding requirement: its widget, rendering, and semantics layers provide much more than a component collection. Web accessibility translates the internal Semantics tree into HTML, but is opt-in by default; I would explicitly enable it and test browser-agent interaction rather than assume canvas rendering is automatically discoverable. Agent-generated UI is also a real integration path: the current A2UI Flutter packages document replacing GenUI. I prefer A2UI as the interface contract because it does not require every client to adopt Flutter; Flutter remains a credible rendering host. Sources: [Flutter repository](https://github.com/flutter/flutter), [web accessibility](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility), [A2UI Flutter integration](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/dart/a2ui_flutter/README.md).

**Ouro UI** — Ouro HX combines copy-in React/Base UI components with unusually concrete interaction constraints: Dialog requires a title, distinguishes controlled and trigger modes, and adapts to a draggable mobile sheet. Ouro AX separately supplies command declarations, typed outcomes, dry runs, attribution, and an external X-ray for agent-facing surfaces; this is materially more than coding-agent documentation. Its Apple offering is real, but the fetched page explicitly says release 0.2.1 contains foundations and the App Intents X-ray, with components still forthcoming and Feel/Reins unreleased. Complete native component coverage and an Android implementation would address my cross-platform objection; I would also preserve the release-pinned tests when customizing copied source. Sources: [Dialog contract](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/dialog.md), [Ouro AX](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/ax.md), [Apple scope and release status](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/apple/).

**Base UI** — An unstyled React behavior foundation with compound parts, portals, and a render prop that merges handlers and refs onto custom elements. This gives me design freedom without reimplementing focus and popup behavior, but also makes correct composition, styling, and application semantics my responsibility. Markdown documentation helps agents build components; it is not itself a runtime action interface. I would choose it for a web component implementation underneath a catalog, not instead of the cross-platform contract. Native adapters and explicit agent-facing operations would be additional layers. Sources: [quick start](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start), [composition rules](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition).

**Vercel UI SDK** — Its architecture is particularly compelling for agents operating existing screens: definePrimitive joins state, actions, and slots over framework-free behaviors, while createAgent exposes snapshot, query, and act through the component API. Agent changes reach normal callbacks with an identifiable source and can be refused, which is much stronger than merely supplying an MCP documentation server. However, the documented adapters target React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components—not native widget frameworks—and the SDK explicitly remains beta. Production-stable APIs and native adapters would make it a much closer choice; today I prefer A2UI’s native rendering reach. Sources: [architecture and beta status](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui), [agent bridge](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent).

**Chakra UI** — createSystem, semantic tokens, recipes, and slot recipes offer a coherent way to constrain a React web design system; strictTokens can prevent arbitrary styling values at type-check time. Its MCP server exposes component props, examples, theme information, and migration assistance, which genuinely improves agent-assisted implementation but does not make the running application agent-operable. The documented component system remains web-oriented, with Emotion as an installation dependency. I would add a runtime tool/action layer and native implementations rather than mistake its framework-agnostic styling engine for native component support. Sources: [theming architecture](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview), [MCP tools](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server), [installation](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui).

**json-render** — A close finalist: defineCatalog constrains components and actions with schemas, defineRegistry supplies implementations, and SpecStream progressively compiles generated specifications. Its current scope genuinely includes React Native alongside several web renderers, plus state bindings, watchers, and MCP integration; dismissing it as web-only would be incorrect. The native renderer source also reveals a concrete recovery trade-off: unknown components return nothing, and component render errors are caught by a boundary that hides the element. I would require visible application-level error reporting and tested catalog parity. I prefer A2UI’s documented SwiftUI/Compose paths and negotiated protocol capabilities over standardizing my native clients on this renderer model. Sources: [packages and specification features](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render), [native renderer implementation](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/src/renderer.tsx).

**MCP Apps** — A stable interoperability and delivery layer: tools reference ui:// HTML resources, compliant hosts render them in sandboxed iframes, and JSON-RPC carries bidirectional interaction. Its explicit CSP and capability negotiation are valuable boundaries, but neither supplies a visual component system nor turns HTML into native controls. Host support and permissions remain negotiated rather than universal. I would use MCP Apps to distribute an interface into compatible assistants, paired with a separate component toolkit; native rendering outside that iframe model would require another layer. Sources: [architecture and supported clients](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps), [stable specification and sandbox requirements](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — My preferred Apple-specific foundation: declarative views, model-to-view data flow, adaptive controls, and HIG guidance provide platform integration rather than a web aesthetic transplanted onto a phone. App Intents separately makes structured actions and entities discoverable to Apple Intelligence, Siri, Shortcuts, and other system experiences; SwiftUI alone should not receive credit for that capability. The decisive limitation is platform scope: this does not supply web or Android rendering. I would share domain operations and schemas while maintaining additional clients, or host A2UI surfaces in SwiftUI. Sources: [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui), [HIG accessibility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility), [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — A focused React/Radix design system with Tailwind 4 tokens and styled controls optimized for ChatGPT apps. Its source makes an important boundary clear: AppsSDKUIProvider currently carries the router link component, not an agent runtime, permissions system, or tool bridge. I would use it to make an embedded ChatGPT surface feel consistent, but would supply the Apps SDK/MCP integration and application authorization separately. Native widget renderers and a less host-specific design layer would be needed before I selected it as the cross-platform foundation. Sources: [features and requirements](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui), [provider implementation](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui/blob/main/src/components/AppsSDKUIProvider/AppsSDKUIProvider.tsx).

**A2UI** — My choice for the shared interface layer, not a claim that one protocol replaces an entire product design system. Core SDKs maintain component graphs and data models, Agent SDKs generate catalog-derived instructions and validate output, and framework adapters render registered components with host-native theming. The current SDK matrix includes web, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose, but explicitly lists Compose at v0.9.1 while other renderers support v1.0; I would negotiate versions rather than assume parity. There are also observed accessibility gaps: SwiftUI group hints and live-region coverage are limited, and Flutter documents explicit-label limitations. I would address these with tested custom catalog implementations, restricted functions, backend authorization, and platform-specific acceptance tests before production. Sources: [SDK architecture and version matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/), [actions and function RPC](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/), [SwiftUI limitations](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md), [Flutter limitations and security](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/dart/a2ui_flutter/README.md).

**MUI** — A comprehensive React web component system whose createTheme, ThemeProvider, component configuration, and CSS-variable support make consistent product styling straightforward. The repository distinguishes its independent Material implementation from Google's system and points to MUI X for more complex controls; I would not equate it with Jetpack Compose Material 3. It offers more ready-made web application structure than a headless primitive library, but neither native widgets nor an agent-operation contract follows from that breadth. Shared domain actions and separate native renderers would address those boundaries; I prefer A2UI for the contract spanning them. Sources: [repository scope](https://github.com/mui/material-ui), [theming architecture](https://mui.com/material-ui/customization/theming/).

**Tamagui** — My strongest conventional web-and-native design-system alternative. Typed tokens, universal styling, an optional optimizing compiler, and Adapt let shared React/React Native components change presentation appropriately; Select documents a common controller spanning browser-native controls, floating lists, and adapted Sheets. This is tangible cross-platform behavior, not just shared color tokens. The trade-off is that compiler/configuration and platform interaction testing still need ownership, while the sources I reviewed do not establish an equivalent framework-independent runtime agent contract. I would add a constrained catalog and shared authorized actions; if React Native were mandatory everywhere, Tamagui would become a particularly attractive foundation. Sources: [architecture and optional compiler](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction), [Select render paths](https://tamagui.dev/ui/select).

**shadcn/ui** — Open component source, composable APIs, a registry schema, and CLI distribution give coding agents inspectable implementations and teams considerable control. The MCP server browses, searches, and installs registry items; that is development-time assistance, not runtime authority over the product. Owning modified component code also means owning update reconciliation and regression testing. The registry has cross-framework distribution support, but that does not establish native parity for its own components. I would use it for web catalog implementations and the AI Elements successor, with separate native components and application actions. Sources: [distribution architecture](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs), [MCP server scope](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — The clearest application-level answer to equal human and agent capabilities: defineAction declares a validated operation that React hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI surfaces all invoke through the same checks and audit path. Shared data and contextual application state reduce the risk of maintaining a second, drifting agent integration. This is a broader TypeScript application framework, however, rather than a native visual component system; the word native describes its agent architecture, not proof of iOS/Android widget rendering. I would adopt its shared-action principle alongside native clients, but would need verified native UI integrations before selecting it over A2UI for this brief. Sources: [repository architecture](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native), [action execution contract](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview).

**Fluent UI** — Fluent spans more than the supplied web repository: the official developer guide documents React v9, FAST-based Web Components, and separate Apple, Android, and Windows implementations. React uses FluentProvider and Griffel, while Web Components use CSS-variable tokens, so the common design language does not mean one shared rendering implementation. That breadth is valuable for Microsoft-aligned products, but I would still coordinate platform packages, component parity, and a separate agent action contract. A shared, tested catalog over those implementations would address my objection; A2UI already supplies that architectural role. Sources: [web repository and migration boundaries](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui), [official cross-platform development guide](https://fluent2.microsoft.design/get-started/develop).

**Radix UI** — A strong low-level React web foundation for focus management, keyboard navigation, and ARIA behavior. Its asChild composition avoids unnecessary wrappers, but custom components must spread props and forward refs, and changing the underlying element can invalidate accessibility. Those are concrete integration obligations for both human and coding-agent authors. It supplies neither native renderer implementations nor the shared runtime operations I need across platforms. I would wrap tested primitives in a constrained web catalog and provide native equivalents rather than treat accessible DOM behavior as a complete agent interface. Sources: [accessibility responsibilities](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/accessibility), [composition contract](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — An excellent Android implementation layer: MaterialTheme centralizes color, typography, and shapes, including dynamic color and Material 3 Expressive support. Compose semantics expose roles, state descriptions, actions, and testing hooks, making interfaces inspectable beyond their pixels; custom controls still need deliberate semantic authoring. The candidate's Android documentation does not by itself establish a shared web renderer or cross-platform agent contract, and some Material APIs require experimental opt-in. I would use it behind A2UI's Compose adapter, while negotiating its supported protocol version, rather than infer universal portability from Kotlin or Material branding. Sources: [Material 3 architecture](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3), [semantics and actions](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics).

**CopilotKit** — A serious agent-interaction stack rather than merely a chat component library: AG-UI streams carry shared state, frontend tools, generative UI, and human-in-the-loop interactions through its runtime. Its React Native support is documented and should not be dismissed as absent, but the quickstart identifies native generative UI as experimental and details Metro, peer-version, and polyfill requirements. I would choose it when agent orchestration and approval flows are the central missing product layer. For this selection, it is broader infrastructure than I need as the shared rendering contract; I would pair it with A2UI or a separate design system, and validate the experimental native path independently. Sources: [architecture and capabilities](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit), [shared-state mechanism](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/shared-state), [React Native integration](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/react-native).

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — A strong web choice where interaction quality and internationalization dominate: React Aria supplies unstyled accessible behavior, Spectrum supplies Adobe's visual system, and React Stately separates reusable state logic. Documented testing spans major desktop and mobile screen readers, with localized strings and direction-aware interactions; application labels, contrast, and target sizes remain the implementer's responsibility. React Stately's potential reuse on React Native is not evidence that React Aria or Spectrum renders native controls. I would use Aria for demanding web catalog components, adding native adapters and authorized agent operations rather than asking web accessibility alone to serve as the entire cross-platform contract. Sources: [library architecture](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum), [accessibility, internationalization, and interaction guarantees](https://react-aria.adobe.com/quality#accessibility).

actions.pullQuote: I’d choose A2UI for its catalog-constrained agent interface and native renderers, while keeping visual design and authorization under application control.
actions.testimonial: I would choose A2UI because its Catalogs and incremental surface updates give agents a bounded interface vocabulary without requiring generated executable UI code. Its Agent SDK, two-way data binding, and bidirectional function RPC let me connect human interactions and agent operations across web, Flutter, and SwiftUI. I would still enforce authorization in application services and test each renderer’s accessibility behavior rather than treating schema validation as a security guarantee. Compared with Tamagui, I accept more catalog implementation and renderer-version coordination in exchange for an explicit, framework-independent agent-to-interface contract.
actions.evaluations:
**AI Elements** — Copy-in React components such as Tool and Confirmation make agent activity legible to people; Tool explicitly represents streaming, approval, completion, denial, and error states. That is a presentation layer, not a native renderer or shared application-operation contract. More importantly for a new project, the captured repository announces deprecation at the end of November 2026 and migration to shadcn/ui. I would use the successor for web conversation surfaces rather than make this repository my foundation; native components and application tools would remain separate work. Sources: [repository and migration notice](https://github.com/vercel/ai-elements), [Tool documentation](https://elements.ai-sdk.dev/components/tool).

**Flutter** — A substantial alternative when one Dart codebase across mobile, desktop, and web is the overriding requirement: its widget, rendering, and semantics layers provide much more than a component collection. Web accessibility translates the internal Semantics tree into HTML, but is opt-in by default; I would explicitly enable it and test browser-agent interaction rather than assume canvas rendering is automatically discoverable. Agent-generated UI is also a real integration path: the current A2UI Flutter packages document replacing GenUI. I prefer A2UI as the interface contract because it does not require every client to adopt Flutter; Flutter remains a credible rendering host. Sources: [Flutter repository](https://github.com/flutter/flutter), [web accessibility](https://docs.flutter.dev/ui/accessibility/web-accessibility), [A2UI Flutter integration](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/dart/a2ui_flutter/README.md).

**Ouro UI** — Ouro HX combines copy-in React/Base UI components with unusually concrete interaction constraints: Dialog requires a title, distinguishes controlled and trigger modes, and adapts to a draggable mobile sheet. Ouro AX separately supplies command declarations, typed outcomes, dry runs, attribution, and an external X-ray for agent-facing surfaces; this is materially more than coding-agent documentation. Its Apple offering is real, but the fetched page explicitly says release 0.2.1 contains foundations and the App Intents X-ray, with components still forthcoming and Feel/Reins unreleased. Complete native component coverage and an Android implementation would address my cross-platform objection; I would also preserve the release-pinned tests when customizing copied source. Sources: [Dialog contract](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/dialog.md), [Ouro AX](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/ax.md), [Apple scope and release status](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/apple/).

**Base UI** — An unstyled React behavior foundation with compound parts, portals, and a render prop that merges handlers and refs onto custom elements. This gives me design freedom without reimplementing focus and popup behavior, but also makes correct composition, styling, and application semantics my responsibility. Markdown documentation helps agents build components; it is not itself a runtime action interface. I would choose it for a web component implementation underneath a catalog, not instead of the cross-platform contract. Native adapters and explicit agent-facing operations would be additional layers. Sources: [quick start](https://base-ui.com/react/overview/quick-start), [composition rules](https://base-ui.com/react/handbook/composition).

**Vercel UI SDK** — Its architecture is particularly compelling for agents operating existing screens: definePrimitive joins state, actions, and slots over framework-free behaviors, while createAgent exposes snapshot, query, and act through the component API. Agent changes reach normal callbacks with an identifiable source and can be refused, which is much stronger than merely supplying an MCP documentation server. However, the documented adapters target React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components—not native widget frameworks—and the SDK explicitly remains beta. Production-stable APIs and native adapters would make it a much closer choice; today I prefer A2UI’s native rendering reach. Sources: [architecture and beta status](https://github.com/vercel-labs/ui), [agent bridge](https://ui-sdk.dev/docs/agents/connect-an-agent).

**Chakra UI** — createSystem, semantic tokens, recipes, and slot recipes offer a coherent way to constrain a React web design system; strictTokens can prevent arbitrary styling values at type-check time. Its MCP server exposes component props, examples, theme information, and migration assistance, which genuinely improves agent-assisted implementation but does not make the running application agent-operable. The documented component system remains web-oriented, with Emotion as an installation dependency. I would add a runtime tool/action layer and native implementations rather than mistake its framework-agnostic styling engine for native component support. Sources: [theming architecture](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/theming/overview), [MCP tools](https://chakra-ui.com/docs/get-started/ai/mcp-server), [installation](https://github.com/chakra-ui/chakra-ui).

**json-render** — A close finalist: defineCatalog constrains components and actions with schemas, defineRegistry supplies implementations, and SpecStream progressively compiles generated specifications. Its current scope genuinely includes React Native alongside several web renderers, plus state bindings, watchers, and MCP integration; dismissing it as web-only would be incorrect. The native renderer source also reveals a concrete recovery trade-off: unknown components return nothing, and component render errors are caught by a boundary that hides the element. I would require visible application-level error reporting and tested catalog parity. I prefer A2UI’s documented SwiftUI/Compose paths and negotiated protocol capabilities over standardizing my native clients on this renderer model. Sources: [packages and specification features](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render), [native renderer implementation](https://github.com/vercel-labs/json-render/blob/main/packages/react-native/src/renderer.tsx).

**MCP Apps** — A stable interoperability and delivery layer: tools reference ui:// HTML resources, compliant hosts render them in sandboxed iframes, and JSON-RPC carries bidirectional interaction. Its explicit CSP and capability negotiation are valuable boundaries, but neither supplies a visual component system nor turns HTML into native controls. Host support and permissions remain negotiated rather than universal. I would use MCP Apps to distribute an interface into compatible assistants, paired with a separate component toolkit; native rendering outside that iframe model would require another layer. Sources: [architecture and supported clients](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps), [stable specification and sandbox requirements](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/specification/2026-01-26/apps.mdx).

**SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines** — My preferred Apple-specific foundation: declarative views, model-to-view data flow, adaptive controls, and HIG guidance provide platform integration rather than a web aesthetic transplanted onto a phone. App Intents separately makes structured actions and entities discoverable to Apple Intelligence, Siri, Shortcuts, and other system experiences; SwiftUI alone should not receive credit for that capability. The decisive limitation is platform scope: this does not supply web or Android rendering. I would share domain operations and schemas while maintaining additional clients, or host A2UI surfaces in SwiftUI. Sources: [SwiftUI](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/swiftui), [HIG accessibility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility), [App Intents](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/appintents).

**OpenAI Apps SDK UI** — A focused React/Radix design system with Tailwind 4 tokens and styled controls optimized for ChatGPT apps. Its source makes an important boundary clear: AppsSDKUIProvider currently carries the router link component, not an agent runtime, permissions system, or tool bridge. I would use it to make an embedded ChatGPT surface feel consistent, but would supply the Apps SDK/MCP integration and application authorization separately. Native widget renderers and a less host-specific design layer would be needed before I selected it as the cross-platform foundation. Sources: [features and requirements](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui), [provider implementation](https://github.com/openai/apps-sdk-ui/blob/main/src/components/AppsSDKUIProvider/AppsSDKUIProvider.tsx).

**A2UI** — My choice for the shared interface layer, not a claim that one protocol replaces an entire product design system. Core SDKs maintain component graphs and data models, Agent SDKs generate catalog-derived instructions and validate output, and framework adapters render registered components with host-native theming. The current SDK matrix includes web, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose, but explicitly lists Compose at v0.9.1 while other renderers support v1.0; I would negotiate versions rather than assume parity. There are also observed accessibility gaps: SwiftUI group hints and live-region coverage are limited, and Flutter documents explicit-label limitations. I would address these with tested custom catalog implementations, restricted functions, backend authorization, and platform-specific acceptance tests before production. Sources: [SDK architecture and version matrix](https://a2ui.org/concepts/sdks/), [actions and function RPC](https://a2ui.org/concepts/actions-and-functions/), [SwiftUI limitations](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/swift/swiftui/README.md), [Flutter limitations and security](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/blob/main/dart/a2ui_flutter/README.md).

**MUI** — A comprehensive React web component system whose createTheme, ThemeProvider, component configuration, and CSS-variable support make consistent product styling straightforward. The repository distinguishes its independent Material implementation from Google's system and points to MUI X for more complex controls; I would not equate it with Jetpack Compose Material 3. It offers more ready-made web application structure than a headless primitive library, but neither native widgets nor an agent-operation contract follows from that breadth. Shared domain actions and separate native renderers would address those boundaries; I prefer A2UI for the contract spanning them. Sources: [repository scope](https://github.com/mui/material-ui), [theming architecture](https://mui.com/material-ui/customization/theming/).

**Tamagui** — My strongest conventional web-and-native design-system alternative. Typed tokens, universal styling, an optional optimizing compiler, and Adapt let shared React/React Native components change presentation appropriately; Select documents a common controller spanning browser-native controls, floating lists, and adapted Sheets. This is tangible cross-platform behavior, not just shared color tokens. The trade-off is that compiler/configuration and platform interaction testing still need ownership, while the sources I reviewed do not establish an equivalent framework-independent runtime agent contract. I would add a constrained catalog and shared authorized actions; if React Native were mandatory everywhere, Tamagui would become a particularly attractive foundation. Sources: [architecture and optional compiler](https://tamagui.dev/docs/intro/introduction), [Select render paths](https://tamagui.dev/ui/select).

**shadcn/ui** — Open component source, composable APIs, a registry schema, and CLI distribution give coding agents inspectable implementations and teams considerable control. The MCP server browses, searches, and installs registry items; that is development-time assistance, not runtime authority over the product. Owning modified component code also means owning update reconciliation and regression testing. The registry has cross-framework distribution support, but that does not establish native parity for its own components. I would use it for web catalog implementations and the AI Elements successor, with separate native components and application actions. Sources: [distribution architecture](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs), [MCP server scope](https://ui.shadcn.com/docs/mcp).

**Agent-native (Builder.io)** — The clearest application-level answer to equal human and agent capabilities: defineAction declares a validated operation that React hooks, agent tools, HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI surfaces all invoke through the same checks and audit path. Shared data and contextual application state reduce the risk of maintaining a second, drifting agent integration. This is a broader TypeScript application framework, however, rather than a native visual component system; the word native describes its agent architecture, not proof of iOS/Android widget rendering. I would adopt its shared-action principle alongside native clients, but would need verified native UI integrations before selecting it over A2UI for this brief. Sources: [repository architecture](https://github.com/BuilderIO/agent-native), [action execution contract](https://agent-native.com/docs/actions-overview).

**Fluent UI** — Fluent spans more than the supplied web repository: the official developer guide documents React v9, FAST-based Web Components, and separate Apple, Android, and Windows implementations. React uses FluentProvider and Griffel, while Web Components use CSS-variable tokens, so the common design language does not mean one shared rendering implementation. That breadth is valuable for Microsoft-aligned products, but I would still coordinate platform packages, component parity, and a separate agent action contract. A shared, tested catalog over those implementations would address my objection; A2UI already supplies that architectural role. Sources: [web repository and migration boundaries](https://github.com/microsoft/fluentui), [official cross-platform development guide](https://fluent2.microsoft.design/get-started/develop).

**Radix UI** — A strong low-level React web foundation for focus management, keyboard navigation, and ARIA behavior. Its asChild composition avoids unnecessary wrappers, but custom components must spread props and forward refs, and changing the underlying element can invalidate accessibility. Those are concrete integration obligations for both human and coding-agent authors. It supplies neither native renderer implementations nor the shared runtime operations I need across platforms. I would wrap tested primitives in a constrained web catalog and provide native equivalents rather than treat accessible DOM behavior as a complete agent interface. Sources: [accessibility responsibilities](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/overview/accessibility), [composition contract](https://www.radix-ui.com/primitives/docs/guides/composition).

**Material 3 and Jetpack Compose** — An excellent Android implementation layer: MaterialTheme centralizes color, typography, and shapes, including dynamic color and Material 3 Expressive support. Compose semantics expose roles, state descriptions, actions, and testing hooks, making interfaces inspectable beyond their pixels; custom controls still need deliberate semantic authoring. The candidate's Android documentation does not by itself establish a shared web renderer or cross-platform agent contract, and some Material APIs require experimental opt-in. I would use it behind A2UI's Compose adapter, while negotiating its supported protocol version, rather than infer universal portability from Kotlin or Material branding. Sources: [Material 3 architecture](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/designsystems/material3), [semantics and actions](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/compose/accessibility/semantics).

**CopilotKit** — A serious agent-interaction stack rather than merely a chat component library: AG-UI streams carry shared state, frontend tools, generative UI, and human-in-the-loop interactions through its runtime. Its React Native support is documented and should not be dismissed as absent, but the quickstart identifies native generative UI as experimental and details Metro, peer-version, and polyfill requirements. I would choose it when agent orchestration and approval flows are the central missing product layer. For this selection, it is broader infrastructure than I need as the shared rendering contract; I would pair it with A2UI or a separate design system, and validate the experimental native path independently. Sources: [architecture and capabilities](https://github.com/CopilotKit/CopilotKit), [shared-state mechanism](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/shared-state), [React Native integration](https://docs.copilotkit.ai/react-native).

**React Aria and React Spectrum** — A strong web choice where interaction quality and internationalization dominate: React Aria supplies unstyled accessible behavior, Spectrum supplies Adobe's visual system, and React Stately separates reusable state logic. Documented testing spans major desktop and mobile screen readers, with localized strings and direction-aware interactions; application labels, contrast, and target sizes remain the implementer's responsibility. React Stately's potential reuse on React Native is not evidence that React Aria or Spectrum renders native controls. I would use Aria for demanding web catalog components, adding native adapters and authorized agent operations rather than asking web accessibility alone to serve as the entire cross-platform contract. Sources: [library architecture](https://github.com/adobe/react-spectrum), [accessibility, internationalization, and interaction guarantees](https://react-aria.adobe.com/quality#accessibility).
